item.title: Types of Thought Distortions and How to Change Your Thinking
item.description:
Thought distortions are patterns of thinking that don’t match reality. Also known as cognitive distortions, they are automatic, inaccurate, often irrational thoughts and beliefs that have little or no evidence to back them up, and that color the way you view yourself, others, and the world, and shape your experiences and behavior.

Types of Thought Distortions

Mental Filtering Mental filtering is zooming in on one negative detail of an experience, frequently taken out of context, while disregarding the broader picture and ignoring everything else about it that is good, positive, or neutral. You do well at school, for instance, but keep beating yourself up and calling yourself stupid because of one question you answered wrong on a test.

Catastrophizing Catastrophizing is when you blow things out of proportion, interpret even harmless situations as frightening, and anticipate the worst, despite having no evidence that such an outcome is possible or even likely. For example, thinking “My son has not called; he must have been in a car accident,” or “This spot on my skin is probably skin cancer.”

Emotional Reasoning Emotional reasoning undermines your logical processes and assumes that what you feel about a situation reflects its reality, regardless of the facts or any evidence to the contrary. For example, “I’m feeling anxious, so something bad must be about to happen,” or “I’m feeling guilty, so I must have done something wrong.

All-Or-Nothing Thinking All-or-nothing thinking is seeing everything in terms of black or white, with no middle ground or shades of gray. Everything is either one extreme or the other, totally perfect or completely bad. A single mistake, for instance, is seen as ruining an entire project, or anything less than an A+ as a failure.

Should Statements “Should” statements are rigid, unrealistic rules you create for yourself using words such as “should,” “should not,” and “must,” that put a lot of pressure on you and lead to guilt and the feeling that you are never enough. “I must make sure the house is spotless before company comes,” for instance, or “I should always know the right thing to say.”

Magnification and Minimization Magnification and minimization are two sides of the same coin. Magnification highlights negatives, exaggerating them and making them seem larger than they are, such as thinking, “I made a mistake at work, so now my whole career is ruined.”

Minimization, on the other hand, diminishes strengths and achievements, making them seem small and insignificant. It can also trivialize important realities, such as ignoring a persistent problem in a relationship and saying, “Everything’s fine, they’re just overreacting.”

Dismissing the Positive Dismissing the positive is discounting the good things that happen to you as not counting, being unimportant or invalid, or chalking them up to luck or coincidence by using disqualifying statements such as, “It was just a lucky guess,” when commended for giving a good answer on a test, or “The only reason I got hired for the job was because the interviewer was desperate to find someone to fill the position.”

Jumping to Conclusions Jumping to conclusions is assuming that something is true or likely to happen, without any evidence to support it. Thinking a friend is angry with you because he is not smiling, for instance, or predicting an outcome there is no basis for, such as “the doctor is going to tell me I have cancer,” when you are on your way for a routine checkup.

Labeling Labeling is judging and defining yourself or someone else negatively, based on an isolated incident or behavior, such as calling yourself an idiot, loser, or failure, because you made a small mistake at work, or calling someone else a jerk, because they accidentally bumped into you.

Overgeneralization Overgeneralization is assuming that one negative event means that all future events will also have negative outcomes and stretching a bad moment into a permanent cycle of defeat, making sweeping assumptions such as, “I misplaced my keys. I can never keep track of anything,” or “I got stuck in traffic this morning. I’ll always be late for work.”

Personalization Personalization is feeling guilty about and blaming yourself for problems that are not your fault, and imagining you caused them even when you had nothing to do with them, or they were issues that were out of your control. Thinking “It’s my fault our team lost the game,” for instance, or “It’s my fault my friend is not enjoying this party.”

Comparisons Comparisons involve comparing yourself or your performance to someone else’s and magnifying your faults and weaknesses while emphasizing their strengths, even when you don’t know all the facts, and then feeling inadequate or inferior and thinking thoughts such as, “All my friends are doing better than I am,” for instance.

Effects of Thought Distortions

Adding to or subtracting from what’s really happening can cloud your judgment, increase stress, and have a detrimental impact on many areas of your life. Catastrophizing over a financial situation or a benign health symptom, for instance, can disrupt your sleep or lead to panic attacks.

Being convinced you’re a failure or that nobody likes you can cause you to isolate and avoid social situations or keep from pursuing new opportunities at work. All-or-nothing thinking and emotional reasoning can lead you to see threats all around you where none exist.

Although everyone tends to have negative thoughts once in a while, if they are constant, they are likely to turn into strongly held beliefs. Left unchecked, a steady flow of negative expectations and predictions can erode your self-esteem, cause you to see yourself as not good enough or unable to change, and lead to frustration, depression, and anxiety.

Causes of Distorted Thinking

In some cases, thought distortions are the brain’s way of looking for mental shortcuts to avoid having to process a lot of information at the same time. Instead of having to deal with future uncertainty, for instance, you make a habit of assuming the worst.

In other cases, distorted thoughts may be your mind’s way of looking for solutions to potential future events, such as the breakup of a relationship or a failing grade at school.

While there is no conclusive evidence of a definitive cause for them, distorted thoughts seem more likely to emerge in times of high stress, and some studies have indicated that people who experience adverse events in childhood, such as financial hardship, abandonment, chronic illness, or trauma, are more vulnerable to distorted thinking as adults.

Tips for Putting an End to Thought Distortions

Identify your thought distortions Becoming aware of and identifying the thought distortions you are most prone to is the first, most important step. It is what enables you to deconstruct them and reframe them in a more positive and realistic way.

Practice nonjudgmental awareness Practice acknowledging your thoughts without judging them or beating yourself up about them.

Question your automatic thoughts Take a closer look at your negative thoughts and ask yourself how rational or realistic they are, if there is any evidence to support them, and if you might be overlooking something positive.

Keep a gratitude journal Look for things you can be thankful for and focus on what is going well in your life without downplaying it. End your day by writing three positive things in your journal that you accomplished or experienced, no matter how small they may seem.

Consider therapy A trained mental health professional can help you identify and address your thought distortions, equip you with tools to reframe and replace them, and help you think in a more balanced way.

item.title: Christian Premarital Counseling: The Framework for Life’s Storms
item.description:
Oh, the naivety of young love. If you’ve been married for a while, this article is not for you. You already know the pitfalls that can come when two become one. You already know, probably firsthand, the challenges that newly married couples face, even those who think that love conquers all. According to John 15:13, “Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.”  But if you’re considering marriage or are already engaged, then please continue to read. Please. For the sake of your marriage and your future and your love and your romantic partner and your family. Please continue to read about the benefits of Christian premarital counseling.

Does Love Conquer All?

No. It most certainly does not. At least not in the way you think it does. God’s love does conquer all. His love restored human communion with the Creator of the universe and saved us all from eternal damnation.  But does your romantic love have the ability to transcend time, change outcomes, and restore all things? Not so much.

Your love for your partner, as pure and intense and selfless as it may seem, does not conquer all the pitfalls you will face during your marriage. Human love, while it is a beautiful, powerful thing, is still fallible, just like the people experiencing it. Love is a good start. It’s a great foundation. It’s even what motivates you to pursue a deeper connection with each other, but it has its limitations.

Assuming that all the obstacles of marriage will be solved by the love you share is naïve. Love will give you the motivation to try to find a solution to your issues, but it will not give you the tools.

You Need Tools: Benefits of Christian Premarital Counseling

You wouldn’t build a house without the right equipment, a blueprint, and some experts in the field. When you get married, you are building a house of sorts. Not a physical building, of course, but the house where your life story will live. Where your heart dwells and where your future will thrive or die.

When you build a house, the most important, fundamental part is the foundation. And as an engaged (or potentially engaged) couple, you need to build a solid, unshakable foundation on which to build the house of your marriage.

Christian premarital counseling gives you the tools to build that firm foundation. It shows you effective ways to communicate with each other and helps you understand your and your partner’s expectations. The costs of happiness in most relationships are attributed to broken communication and financial stress and strain. Having such a framework helps you frame whether these expectations are reasonable, biblical, and healthy.

Your counselor will help you talk about sensitive topics like physical intimacy, past relationships, integration of families, financial issues, and future plans without letting tension erode the relationship.

The Practical Skills You’ll Learn

Some people think that premarital counseling is just a designated place to talk about problems in the relationship. But the reality is that it goes way beyond that by giving you the methodology to solve them. You’ll learn skills for identifying your negative interaction cycle, such as pursue and withdraw, how to use “I Statements” effectively, and a guide to structured problem-solving that helps to keep emotional reactions in check.

Discovering new and interesting things about your partner is what keeps the spark lit. Through premarital counseling, you will learn how to maintain curiosity about your partner. While becoming “comfortable” with each other is often the goal because it can bring peace, the unfortunate flip side to that story is that it can also lead to boredom if curiosity isn’t maintained.

That’s why it’s important to continue to see your partner as an evolving person with new ideas, dreams, and challenges. Premarital counseling equips you with techniques to continuously ask intentional, open-ended questions to keep the interest and intrigue alive and help keep the fires burning.

Expectations Vs. Reality

Everyone has their vision of ideal love. As a child, you might read fairy tales about a prince and a charming maiden who live “happily ever after.” But that expectation is rooted in fantasy, not reality. The reality is that even people in the healthiest relationships who carry unspoken expectations are setting themselves and their intended up for disaster.

What a “good spouse” does, how holidays should work, how often you see family, how affection is shown, who handles what at home… the list goes on and on. Most people don’t even know that they have these subtle and hidden expectations until they’re not met because they’re often wrapped in their memories and experiences.

Much of what you learn to be “absolute truths” and relational structures is established in your childhood. How did your dad treat your mom? Did your parental figures act romantic toward each other, or did they live as roommates? How were chores divided? By traditional gender roles?

Premarital counseling helps you drag those hidden expectations out into the light. You’ll talk about your expectations surrounding communication, conflict (and resolution), chores, faith, money, emotional needs, and even how each of you defines respect. Even when you know what your partner expects, meeting those expectations can be difficult. But if you at least understand each other better, you can strive toward meeting or negotiating them.

Preparing for Life’s Storms with Christian Premarital Counseling in Washington

Every couple walks into their engagement with excitement, hope, and a few stars in their eyes. And that optimism is a beautiful thing because God did design love to be joyful. But life, even really good lives, isn’t immune to pitfalls and obstacles. Eventually, illness, financial strain, job loss, grief, infertility, parenting challenges, spiritual drought, or just the stresses and exhaustion of everyday life can shake even the strongest couples.

Christian premarital counseling in Washington state gives you the chance to talk honestly about how you each handle stress, disappointment, and fear before you’re standing in the thick of it. You’ll learn how to support each other during hardship without shutting down or getting angry, blaming, or withdrawing. You’ll learn how to lean on each other instead of letting these things pull you apart.

Dealing With Others

When you’re in love, it feels like you and your spouse are on your own little continent, where the whole world fades into the background, and it seems like nothing and no one else matters. But that’s not reality. Marriage doesn’t happen in a vacuum. As wonderful as that “just us” bubble feels now, real life will eventually burst it.

You will interact with people of the opposite sex. So will your partner. Premarital counseling will help you decide on boundaries with the opposite sex now, while you’re still in the “honeymoon phase.” You will learn how to handle these relationships with transparency and in ways that meet each other’s needs and help you and your partner feel secure.

You will also learn how to handle relationships with in-laws, coworkers, friends, church members, neighbors, and people your spouse knew long before they knew you, because all of these connections, healthy and complicated, will influence your marriage in some way.

You Need God

God wants to help you have a successful marriage.

God is the author of love, even romantic love. He created Eve as a special gift to Adam. The Bible is full of stories of commitment and covenant. Christ’s sacrificial and selfless love for the church is the ultimate template for how a husband is to love his wife (Ephesians 5).

Chrisitan premarital counseling can be part of God’s plan to help your future marriage succeed. In Proverbs, it says, “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22 NIV). And that’s really the heart of premarital counseling. That’s really the heart of God.

You don’t have to walk blindly and figure life out on your own. God wants to walk with you into this big life-changing thing called marriage. And to that end, He has placed resources around you, tools, such as counselors, mentors, and of course, the Bible. He has offered His Holy Spirit as a guide. You just have to choose to accept the help and the wisdom He has made available to you.

What To Do When Love Doesn’t Conquer All

You need to acknowledge that your human love, as beautiful and intense as it is, is insufficient by itself. You need to willingly bring outside wisdom, both human (counseling) and divine (Scripture and the Holy Spirit), into your union before the crisis hits.

When you make the conscious decision to pursue premarital counseling, you are honoring God by seeking the “many advisers” He promised would lead to success. You’re committing to building your house not just on good feelings and mutual interests, but on the Solid Rock of eternal wisdom and covenant love.

Contact us today to schedule a Christian premarital counseling appointment with a Christian counselor in Washington state who can help you begin your marriage on a strong foundation.

item.title: Beyond Guilt and Shame: Christian Counseling for Externally Oriented Struggles
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself standing in the middle of your closet, surrounded by clothes with price tags still attached? Maybe you find yourself scrolling through social media and comparing your home to what you see in the photos. Materialism isn’t as simple as wanting nice things; consequently, the pursuit of material things often becomes a prison of guilt and shame. This prison is not how God designed us to live.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you – Matthew 6:33, ESV

Many Christians today struggle with the weight of materialism that previous generations had never encountered. Our culture today screams from every direction about how our worth is measured by what we own or don’t own.

From what we wear to the house we live in, we are under a constant barrage of temptations to compare. This message seeps into our thoughts and creates a battlefield between what we know is not true and what the world says is important.

The Spiritual Trap of Materialism

We often think of materialism in terms of someone greedy or obsessed with wealth. The truth is that materialism is much more subtle, especially for Christians, who seek to follow God’s heart.

Materialism isn’t just about having nice things. It is where we place our security, our hope, and our identity. It is how we often measure success in today’s world. This is how material possessions begin to fill spaces that were designed for God to occupy.

We don’t need to live in shame or feel guilty about the blessings that He gives to us. Scripture tells us that every good and perfect gift comes from Him. It is not in receiving these gifts that we become entangled in materialism, but rather when we make those gifts our god. When we place our happiness and security in what we can buy and acquire or display, we have shifted from spiritual to worldly living.

Once we are entangled in this, it becomes a vicious cycle. We find ways to convince ourselves that we need the things we see. And in that justification, we acquire it and feel satisfied for a fleeting moment. Then we become overwhelmed with guilt, asking ourselves, “Did I need this? Could the money have been spent better? What will people think?” That’s followed by the shame when we hear, “You’re not a good steward. “You’re selfish.”

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. – Matthew 6:19-21, ESV

The Pattern of Guilt and Shame in Material Pursuit

To overcome the cycle associated with material pursuit, it is important to understand the difference between guilt and shame. We feel guilty about our purchasing desires or inability to be content. We then compare ourselves to others who seem to have less and feel guilty for wanting more.

This thought process leads us to look at credit card statements and feel guilty about our choices. Yet underneath all the guilt, shame is at work, whispering destructive lies about who we are.

Shame, on the other hand, tells us we’re greedy when we are simply human. Shame tells us we’re bad stewards when we are learning to navigate a chaotic and complex world. It then tells us we are failures as Christians because we struggle with contentment.

These thoughts trap us in a cycle and can lead to other issues, such as emotional issues, eating, shopping binges, and isolation.

Spiritually, the impact of guilt and shame cannot be understated. As we constantly battle these emotions, we find it harder to pray, read scripture, and believe that God delights in us. This leads to avoiding fellowship because we fear others will see through our disguise to the real image.

We may even stop tithing or giving because we are too guilty about our spending. This is where we find that the very relationship that could set us free has become clouded by the shame and guilt that we carry.

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus – Romans 8:1, ESV

God Desires for Us to Be Free from Condemnation

God’s heart toward us is not one of disappointment regarding our struggle with materialism. He does not want to see us bound by guilt and shame. He is not sitting in judgment of a credit card statement or an Amazon cart. What He does see are His children, whom He adores, who are learning to navigate a world that consistently pulls them away from Him.

The difference between conviction and condemnation plays a crucial role in freedom from materialism. Conviction is when the Holy Spirit gently nudges and redirects us toward God’s desired plans for us. Condemnation is the harsh voice of the enemy that beats us down and leads us into hiding from God. Condemnation drives us away, but conviction draws us to God.

When we are feeling convicted about materialism, it is not to shame us; it is meant to set us free. God knows that when our hearts are tangled up in the pursuit of things, we miss out on His joy and peace.

He is not angry with the struggle we have, and He doesn’t show disappointment. He desires to see us walk in freedom from the vicious bondage of materialism. It is His love that compels Him to bring correction that will make changes in our lives.

God wants to provide not only our needs, but He also wants to bless us in abundance. It’s not that He doesn’t want us to have nice things. It’s that He wants us to have an identity in Him rather than belongings. When we are anchored in His love for us, we receive blessings with gratitude and hold them lightly because we know that our treasure is in heaven and not in the world.

The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. – Zephaniah 3:17, ESV

How Christian Counseling Provides a Healing Pathway

Anyone struggling with guilt and shame from materialistic patterns does not have to carry the burden alone. Christian Counseling can offer a path to healing that addresses not just the symptoms but the root causes of the struggle.

Secular counseling often focuses on behavior modification, but biblical counseling will recognize that material struggles are often symptoms of deeper emotional needs.

A Christian counselor can help with identifying the lies about worth, security, and identity that have been believed. Using Scripture, these counselors can guide us to discover God’s truth about our identity and how God sees us.

Using a faith-based plan, Christian counselors can help develop practical strategies for managing the triggers and making wise financial decisions. This will lead to contentment in building a relationship with God.

Some practical steps that may be included in faith-based Christian Counseling are:

  • Learning to pause before purchasing and ask God about the purchase.
  • Developing gratitude to shift focus from what you lack to your blessings.
  • Create accountability and relationships with other believers,
  • Establish financial boundaries that reflect values rather than impulses.

The goal of overcoming guilt and shame from materialism isn’t for us to live in deprivation. The main goal is freedom to make decisions from a place of peace rather than compulsion. This freedom allows us to enjoy God’s blessings without guilt and shame because we know our security is from Him.

Living in Freedom

God understands we live in a world where success is measured by one’s belongings. This is not how he intended for us to live. God’s plan has always included freedom and blessings of abundance. The mentality of guilt and shame comes from an enemy who wants to see us bound.

If you or someone you know is trapped in patterns of guilt and shame involving materialism, reach out to a local Christian counselor. Freedom can become a part of everyday life, replacing the shackles of guilt and shame.

item.title: Counseling for Children: “That’s Not Fair!”
item.description:
“That’s not fair!” If you’re a parent, you’ve probably heard that phrase many times, and recently. Children use it to plead their case when you make a decision that they disagree with. They might scream at you as they are carried away from the playground or mumble it as you unplug their favorite device.

Your child, of course, is using the phrase, “that’s not fair,” to express their feelings of disapproval and frustration in their lack of power. But what they aren’t doing is fully comprehending what the term means. That’s not too surprising, because a lot of people, even adults, don’t understand it. The phrase is often used to mean getting what you want, expecting equal outcomes, or expressing frustration, but that’s not what fairness is.

Is that distinction important? Especially at an early age? Yes. An early understanding of fairness shapes social skills, moral reasoning, and the ability and desire to follow rules. Misunderstanding the concept of fairness can lead to issues with entitlement or frustration.

How Fairness is Misunderstood

Many people, children and adults alike, confuse fairness with getting what they want. A child might argue that it’s not fair that their sibling gets more time online. But what they might not understand is that the older sibling’s privilege is often a fair outcome rooted in age appropriateness or their demonstrated effort in following household rules, rather than a mere arbitrary gift.

The word fair, as defined by Merriam-Webster, is: “marked by impartiality and honesty: free from self-interest, prejudice, or favoritism.”

Pause a moment on that phrase, “marked by impartiality and honesty: free from self-interest, prejudice or favoritism.” That means that for something to be fair, it must first be rooted in honesty and equality, not simply whether the outcome is what you wanted it to be or not.

Fairness considers each person’s intrinsic and inalienable rights. Those things they are entitled to, based on their position in life, honesty, responsibility, effort, and age appropriateness, are what determine what is fair.

Biblical Meaning

The dictionary definition of fairness aligns with what the Bible teaches. In James 3:17, it says, “But the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.” (NIV) Fairness, then, is directly connected to God’s wisdom. Fairness means treating people with honesty, kindness, and without favoritism, as God models and instructs.

The Bible also warns not to confuse fairness with favoritism and links a person’s actions to a just outcome without prejudice. In James 2:1-9, “My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism… If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.” (NIV)

This passage is powerful because it speaks of the core concept of true fairness, that outcomes are determined by outside factors, choices, and universal truths, not by self-interest or special treatment. It establishes an absolute, impartial rule. If a person does something wrong, they will be repaid for their wrong. Their repayment is the fair consequence or impartial results, but not necessarily pleasant.

Fairness is about honesty. God cares deeply that our actions and decisions reflect truth, not deception or manipulation. Proverbs 11:1(NIV) says: “The Lord detests dishonest scales, but accurate weights find favor with him.”

Applying that to the definition of fairness, being fair is not really about what you give or even receive, but it’s about the integrity behind your decision. Just like God measures things honestly, you too are called to be honest in how you treat others, even when it might be easier to favor one person over another.

How The Misconception Affects Children

Is establishing a true definition of fairness and instilling that in your children really that important? Yes, because a convoluted view of fairness can trickle down and affect every area of their life, from how they perceive the way others treat them to the consequences they expect and their work ethic.

Children need to realize that fairness is not a guarantee of happiness, but rather a reflection of justice. If your child is angry that you held to your word and gave them half an hour on the playground, they need to realize that their anger doesn’t make the decision unfair because they were given what they were promised. And if you decide to extend their time on the playground, that is not fairness, but generosity.

Consider a teenager who gets upset because you’ve limited them to one hour of screen time a day. They might insist that “it isn’t fair” and feel frustrated. However, the key to their understanding of the concept of fairness is recognizing the distinctions between rights and privileges. Fairness doesn’t apply to what was never guaranteed in the first place. By setting a limit, you are being generous in allowing the privilege at all, not unfair by restricting it.

And that brings us to the issue of entitlement. Just because you want something doesn’t mean you’re entitled to it. Fairness is about justice, integrity, and consistency, not just granting every desire. When children internalize this, they learn to appreciate boundaries, respect rules, and see that generosity is a gift, separate from what is deserved or owed.

Reframing Fairness

If your family is struggling with issues of entitlement or a misconception about fairness, consider seeking therapy. A therapist can work with your child to transition them from an outcome-based definition of fairness to an integrity-based definition. By showing them that fairness doesn’t mean that they get what they want, but rather what they deserve, they will learn about gratitude, hard work, and integrity.

A therapist can also help your child categorize things like food and safety as inalienable and guaranteed rights, and screen time or toys as privileges they either earn or are gifted. A therapist can also help link action to consequence through role-playing and help the child process feelings of frustration.

What many call “fair” is just a veneer for favoritism

The popular definition of fairness can often refer to favoritism or generosity. Favoritism subverts the essence of true fairness because it injects partiality into the outcome and removes reality and responsibility. It directly violates the core principles of the fairness you’re teaching your children because it introduces the idea of partiality and prejudice into the outcome.

Children, whether they’re expecting reward or leniency, need to learn that fairness, not favoritism, is based on integrity, inalienable rights, effort, responsibility, and other, more complicated factors, not just arbitrary preferences or instant gratification. In teaching your children the right mindset surrounding fairness, you’re also teaching them about graciousness and generosity.

Peppered among your hardline rules and consequences is a softer space reserved for grace. Because while consistent absolutes are important, it’s also valuable for children to see that kindness and fairness can coexist.

The message of salvation illustrates the ultimate example of fairness and generosity. We are sinners and deserve judgment. But God, in his unwavering and omnipotent love for us, gave the most generous sacrifice so we can live eternally. Not because we are worthy or because it’s our right, but because of His generosity and love.

God created a way for us to escape the punishment that was fair for us to receive and interrupted that with generosity. And that lesson of justice and generosity can lead your child closer to a life of integrity and a closer walk with God.

To learn more about teaching fairness and mercy to your children, contact our office today to schedule a meeting with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory.

item.title: PTSD and Relationships: How You Can Find Hope by Healing Together
item.description:
Trauma doesn’t stay contained to one person. PTSD and relationships are often intertwined because of the effects of post-traumatic stress. This ripples out and touches the people closest to you. Partners, friends, and family members often navigate the unfamiliar territory of emotional distance and protective walls within these relationships. The person they love has built barriers that feel impossible to cross because of trauma.

This isn’t about understanding what PTSD is. The challenge involves recognizing how the trauma will reshape how you connect, trust, and feel safe with others around you. The result is complex, where the survivor and their loved ones try to bridge a gap.

Both people involved may feel stuck, unsure of how to help each other without making things worse. There is hope when both people are willing to walk toward healing and restoration, instead of surviving the trauma.

When Trauma Changes How Someone Connects

PTSD can alter the way a person experiences a relationship. The brain’s response to trauma has created a pattern of hypervigilance, emotional numbing, and avoidance that was not there before. Some may retreat into silence, while others may pull away from physical touch. These changes aren’t character flaws or choices; they are survival mechanisms. The brain developed an automatic survival response to protect itself from perceived danger.

When the survivor’s protective response clashes with the partner’s need for connection, there’s a difficult balance that has emerged. One person is trying to feel safe by creating distance, and the other is feeling abandoned and confused because of the withdrawal. Both people are hurting, and neither one is wrong. The result becomes a cycle in which one person seeks more connection, and the other withdraws more, leaving the relationship feeling as though it’s unraveling.

There are times when both people blame themselves, which makes the situation more painful. The survivor feels guilty for not being able to get over it, and the partner wonders what they did wrong. PTSD isn’t about blame, it is about a brain that has been rewired by trauma and needs compassionate support to find long-term healing. Recognizing this distinction is often the first step toward finding a way forward together.

It’s always good to remember God’s promises about healing. In Psalm 147, we are reminded how He handles our broken, wounded places: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NIV)

The Hidden Impact on Partners and Loved Ones

Most of the attention focuses on the person with PTSD, which can leave their loved ones experiencing their own form of trauma. Secondary traumatic stress is real, and when families absorb the emotional weight of someone else’s pain, it can take a toll. These family members experience their own anxiety, depression, and exhaustion from constantly managing a crisis.

Christian counselors can provide crucial support for both individuals. This form of counseling helps partners understand that caring for themselves doesn’t diminish their commitment to their loved one. A partner who is emotionally healthy and spiritually grounded is far better equipped to offer steady, compassionate support over long-term healing.

The capacity to be present over the long haul is strengthened as they find that setting boundaries, expressing needs, and seeking support are acts of wisdom, not selfishness. It is how they can follow the guidance in Galatians: “Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:2, NIV)

Rebuilding Trust When PTSD and Relationships Collide

One of the first struggles of PTSD and relationships is trust. Trauma has taught the brain that the world is dangerous and people cannot be trusted. Even though a partner has done nothing to warrant distrust, the survivor’s nervous system remains on high alert and interprets neutral actions as threats. A delayed text response may begin to register as evidence of abandonment. Anger or rejection can be read into certain tones in the other person’s voice.

Rebuilding trust requires patience that often feels unimaginable. It involves the partners consistently showing up, remaining steady, and not taking the distrust personally, even when it hurts. The survivor is required to work on recognizing when their trauma responses are distorting reality. This isn’t a quick process, and there will be setbacks, but progress is possible when both people are committed to the healing process.

Christian counselors are trained to help couples develop practical strategies for trust building. These strategies include creating predictable routines to help the survivor feel safe and practicing transparent communication to reduce misunderstandings. In some cases, it may require establishing check-in rituals that ensure connection without becoming codependent. Small, consistent actions are the foundations that will enable trust to grow again.

Communication Strategies that Honor Both Hearts

When PTSD and relationships collide, communication is often the first thing to break down. The survivor faces challenges articulating what they are feeling or needing, especially during heightened emotional flooding or a flashback. The partners ask questions or offer solutions that may feel invasive or dismissive, even though they are only trying to help. Each person ends up frustrated and more disconnected.

Effective communication and trauma recovery start with recognizing that a survivor in a triggered state cannot engage in rational conversation. These moments require grounding and safety instead of resolution. Partners must learn to offer a calm presence rather than trying to fix the problem.

Finding a rhythm for communication works best when it happens outside of the hard moments. Couples can carve out intentional times to talk through difficult topics or lean on written communication when face-to-face conversations feel like too much.

Christian counselors guide couples in finding the approaches that work for their unique dynamic. This creates a communication style that honors both individuals, where trauma survivors find safety and partners feel heard.

There are also opportunities for deeper spiritual connections that result from navigating these conversations. Praying as a couple and acknowledging dependence on God’s guidance becomes a shared practice that quietly strengthens the relationship over time. Scripture reading offers wisdom that reminds them both that they are not alone in their challenges.

Hope for Healing Together

Even though PTSD creates real challenges in a relationship, it does not have to be the end of connection and intimacy. When the survivor and their loved one approach healing with honesty, patience, and professional support, these relationships can deepen and strengthen beyond simply surviving. This journey isn’t linear, and there will be difficult days, but each small step forward and each moment of vulnerability can build toward lasting hope.

Faith offers a foundation that will sustain a couple through this process. When both people acknowledge they are not alone, that God is present in their healing, and that healing is possible through His grace, they find the strength needed to persevere through this healing journey.

Christian counselors integrate the spiritual dimension and evidence-based trauma treatment to address the psychological and spiritual aspects of recovery such as Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), Somatic Experiencing, and/or Internal Family System (IFS). This combination addresses not just the symptoms of trauma but the deeper wounds that affect how a person relates to God, to themselves, and to the people they love.

This builds hope that something new can emerge, rather than simply returning to what existed before the trauma. Healing for this couple won’t happen in isolation. It requires that they reach out for help and choose courage over fear one day at a time.

If PTSD is affecting your relationship, you do not have to navigate this journey alone. You can contact our office and connect with experienced Christian counselors who understand trauma recovery and relationship healing.

item.title: Divorce and Children: What Your Kids Want You to Know About Their Emotional Needs
item.description:
No one plans on getting divorced when they say, “I do.” But life happens. Previous family-of-origin cultural norms and communication styles can tend to stand at the forefront of unresolved issues. Circumstances change, and people can grow apart, with unresolved resentment and unforgiveness. When people begin to only exist in their marriage, interactions and healthy communication will become difficult, and sometimes divorce may become unavoidable.

While divorce can be a trauma for the adults going through it, it can have an even bigger impact on the children involved. Depending on the age of the child, normally they do not have the emotional vocabulary to express their discomfort watching their parents’ struggle. Interestingly, children see and feel the uneasiness parents are experiencing but are not saying. It is true, actions do speak louder than words.

What do your children want you to know as they go through this crisis with you? Right, it is not just you and your spouse who are experiencing internal turmoil. Wouldn’t it be great if you could read your children’s minds? Understand their fears?

Then you would know how to comfort them. What to say. You’d know how to reassure them and offer hope and comfort for the upcoming changes that will require a sense of safety mentally, emotionally, and physically, so that your love will remain.

Some children may be able to express their innermost thoughts and feelings, but most lack the emotional maturity, vocabulary, and self-awareness needed to communicate their emotions truly. As a parent, you may not understand why they are acting out.

Here’s what your children may want to express to you. The letters below depict what a child may think or feel during the divorce process. Read them and consider how these thoughts and feelings may relate to your child.

I’m confused

Dear Mom and Dad,

You know what’s going on between the two of you. You know how the divorce process works, but I don’t. I don’t have the life experience you do, so the only idea of what a divorce is comes from what some of my friends say at school and a few movies I’ve seen. And it hasn’t been good.

I literally don’t know what’s going on. Attorney? Custody? These are all just foreign words to me, and I have no idea what they mean or if I even need to learn them.

All I know is that it’s really bad. I thought we had a good family. I don’t know what happened. I know you were arguing, and it was loud. Mom would cry, one of you would slam a door or leave the house, but you came back. I know you have been distant from each other, but I don’t know when you stopped loving each other. And if you can stop loving each other, what would prevent you from stopping loving me?

Love,
Your Child

Divorce is confusing, even when you’re the adult going through it. This is even more true when you’re a child who is being dragged along with no vote or power into the unknown. Not only is the situation scary, but it’s uncertain. There are many unanswered questions that the child doesn’t know to ask or is afraid to ask. They may be feeling left out or abandoned.

Even the terminology that gets tossed around during divorce proceedings can be confusing for everyone except for maybe your lawyer and the judge. Unless you’ve been through it before, you’re not likely to be an expert in divorce proceedings, so imagine how disorienting this whole new, scary world is for your child, who has even less life experience.

Take the time to talk with your child about your marriage and what is happening. Kids need honesty, but they need age-appropriate honesty. Tell them that the trouble your family is facing isn’t their fault and that you’re still figuring out the details.

Give them the child-sized version of the situation. They will appreciate your honesty. It will help to orient them. It is important to inform your children before there is a court date. You may wish to seek professional help for this step.

I need stability

Dear Mom and Dad,

I know we’re going through a transition as a family; sometimes I feel like I’m lost. I love you both, but I feel guilty sometimes. Does this mean I have to choose? This sucks. Are we still family? Probably not. Sometimes I feel like I’ve been in a really bad earthquake and everything around me has fallen to the ground.

Yeah, after earthquakes, people rebuild slowly, but we are not a building; we are a family – or at least we used to be. New buildings look good, but how do you rebuild your family? What do I rebuild with? What is going to be strong enough since our family wasn’t strong enough when the earthquake hit?

With everything changing in my world, I need the tremors to stop so I can orient myself in this new life. Does this mean we have to move away from my friends, my neighborhood, or my grandparents? Please don’t make me change schools or give up my room. I need something familiar, something to hold onto when everything around me is changing.

Love,

Your Child

A change in lifestyle is practically inevitable during a divorce. Separating lives means moving into new places, changing your schedules, and editing your social circle. Just because your life is changing doesn’t mean theirs has to. It’s important not to change theirs unnecessarily. Try to maintain some semblance of normalcy for your children during this tumultuous time.

Help them maintain the good parts of their lives that they’re used to. Just because you’re angry with the in-laws doesn’t mean that you should pull your children away from the comfort of their familiarity. Just because going to a certain restaurant triggers painful memories in you doesn’t mean that you should ban your children from it.

And just because you desperately want to integrate your new love interest into your life, doesn’t mean your children are ready for it. We shouldn’t deny them the opportunity to heal. Learn to be self-aware of your internal feelings, thoughts, and reactions as well as those of your children. Each of you are experiencing grief and loss. Your grief and loss may be experienced differently, but they are experienced.

Never put your child in the position to choose sides or become a secret agent gathering information on the other parent during or after the divorce proceeding. You will be setting yourself up for more pain and discomfort.

Many parents make the unfortunate mistake of pitting their children against the other parent. It’s quite natural for humans to try to rally support in the midst of a crisis or try to convince others that their actions are justified or that they are the victim. But this is not your child’s job. Don’t make your children into soldiers, spies, or your emotional support team. They are children, and they deserve to have an uninterrupted relationship with both parents.

I need permission to express my emotions

Dear Mom and Dad,

Sometimes I feel guilty when I enjoy being with one of you. I don’t want the other person to be sad or feel left out. I don’t want to cause you more hurt. So sometimes I pretend to be less happy than I am. Sometimes I pretend to be happy when I’m not.

Please tell me it’s okay to smile, laugh, and have fun with both of you. Please tell me that loving one parent doesn’t mean that I’m betraying the other. Tell me I can cry when I feel it without upsetting you.

Love,

Your Child

Children feel responsible for protecting their parents’ feelings. They might hide joy, affection, or excitement because they think it’ll hurt the other parent. They might suppress tears so they don’t stress you out. Tell them that you’re glad when they spend time with the other parent and that you know they love you, even when they’re not with you.

Give your child permission to cry or even be angry. This allows them to be wholly invested in both parental relationships. It gives them the freedom to be authentic in their emotions and authentic with you.

Consider taking your child to a Christian therapist who will help them understand their emotions. Therapy can give them a platform to discuss how they feel without worrying about how it might affect either parent. A therapist can give them space to feel and live authentically and provide coping skills to use when things feel overwhelming.

Moving Forward

What would your child tell you as you go through a divorce? They would tell you that they want you to be happy, but they don’t want to be responsible for it. They would tell you they love you both and that they need more help than they feel they can ask for.

Divorce may change the structure of your family, but it doesn’t have to destroy your child’s life. God gave you your children as a precious gift. As their parents, it’s your job to be a good steward of that gift. Pay attention to what their actions are conveying because they don’t always have the confidence or vocabulary to verbally tell you themselves.

Help them find the help they need through therapy and reassure them that no matter what happens, God still loves them and wants to help. Put your children’s hearts first so they can emerge from the divorce with the same innocence they had before, but with more coping skills and a renewed assurance that they’re loved.

Contact our reception team today to schedule an appointment with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory. You can also seek positive support through your church or Christian divorce support groups.

item.title: The Case for Premarital Counseling
item.description:
Major life decisions require time and wisdom to be effectively navigated. If something is going to affect you in the long term, or if it’s going to have a huge impact on your life, it warrants meaningful consideration. You don’t want to make a rash decision that significantly affects your well-being and the rest of your life. Premarital counseling is one of the ways couples can meaningfully explore the complex and important question of marriage.

If two people are planning on getting married, doing premarital counseling may not be high on their list of priorities. Their attention could be drawn by other concerns that feel more pressing, such as venues, caterers, vendors, deposits, color schemes, the guest list, and the seemingly endless tasks that come with a wedding. These things rightfully clamor for attention, and it’s easy to see them as making or breaking the couple’s special day.

Premarital counseling can feel like an unwelcome intrusion amid this flurry of activity. Depending on what a person has heard about premarital counseling, it can feel like a roadblock or even an unnecessary exercise for your relationship. It’s helpful to describe what premarital counseling is and its role for a couple.

Different types of counseling help individuals and couples navigate aspects of their lives and relationships. The aim is to help them discover patterns and habits of thought and behavior that promote or undermine well-being. The counseling process helps the couple or individual identify these and learn new ways of thinking or doing things. This is all in an effort to help them flourish.

When it comes to premarital counseling, it’s a structured time and process of walking with a couple to explore their readiness for marriage in a practical as well as biblical manner. One way to think of what premarital counseling does for the couple is that it operates like a mirror and a guide for them relationally.

Like a mirror held up to your face reflects it and shows you what you look like, the premarital counseling process reflects the realities of the relationship. This helps the couple see their strengths as well as areas for growth in the relationship. These are sometimes called blind spots. Much like a person cannot see their blind spots unless they intentionally turn and give attention, a person cannot acknowledge or address concerns until intentionality and action occur.

Premarital counseling also functions as a guide for the couple. Beyond identifying the strengths and areas for growth, your counselor will also provide you with a biblical foundation for understanding marriage and its purpose.

These biblical principles, as well as practical strategies, are essential for building a Christ-centered and Christ-honoring marriage. God loves and honors marriage. He uses the illustration of a bride and bridegroom to signal the importance of His covenant relationship with His people.

The Blessing and Responsibility of Marriage

For believers in Jesus, marriage is a joyfully serious matter. It’s not the sort of relationship a person should enter lightly. The other part of the equation is that marriage is meant to be a blessing for the couple, a source of companionship, shared growth, and joy. As a special kind of bond and commitment between two people, marriage reflects Jesus’ own love for His church (Ephesians 5:32), making it a beautiful blessing.

While it is a blessing, marriage is not without its responsibilities. It’s a rather long passage, but 1 Corinthians 7 tries to set out the realities of married and single life. Our lives are meant to honor the Lord regardless of whether we’re married or not, but the apostle is clear that married life brings potential distractions and responsibilities. These can take away from an exclusive focus on the work of the kingdom.

Marriage requires a lot from a person, including patience, commitment, and selflessness every day. This doesn’t detract from either the ups or the downs. Marriage blesses a person as a source of emotional and spiritual support, a space to share life with a companion, and the opportunity to serve the Lord together. Marriage is also a foundation for a family and a legacy that could extend over generations.

Just as marriage has its blessings and responsibilities, it also has significant challenges. Some of these challenges include balancing family expectations and obligations with your own desires. When married, you’re no longer your own, and that can bring tension when your desires are at odds with your partner.

Other challenges that could arise within marriage include managing the financial responsibilities that come with the relationship and a family. A family requires more financial resources to sustain, and that could be a pressure point for a couple.

A couple can also face the challenge of misalignment. This misalignment may be regarding their life goals. How they handle spirituality and worship, how to handle their money, the rules around social media engagement, whether to have friends of the opposite sex, how to relate to in-laws, whether to have kids and how many, expectations about sex, roles in the home, and different ways of engaging in conflict.

Lastly, marriages often face the challenge of coping with differences in personality and preferences between the spouses. One spouse might be outgoing while the other is a homebody. Spouses may differ on issues of discipline, how to relate to their children, or even how to spend their time and money. These challenges can be the source of deep conflict in a marriage.

How Premarital Counseling Helps Couples

Premarital counseling helps couples in several important ways. This is tied to the kinds of things that a couple talks through with their counselor during their sessions. Premarital counseling encourages the couple to engage in honest and vulnerable conversation about their values and expectations for the marriage. Couples may mask these, but doing so only causes problems as the years go by.

As couples share about themselves, their relationship, and more, they can also identify potential areas of conflict. If a couple has different expectations about family time, that could be the source of conflict in the future when they are figuring out where, how, and with whom to spend the holidays. It’s better to get ahead of these topics and deal with them before they derail the relationship.

Conflict is a reality in every relationship. However, conflict can vary depending on how the couple handles it and how often it recurs. One of the things premarital counseling does is to equip the couple with tools for mutual spiritual growth, financial goal setting and planning, as well as healthy conflict resolution. Knowing how to handle conflict is a valuable life skill and makes for a healthier relationship.

Premarital counseling also helps couples grasp the seriousness of marriage as a lifelong covenant before the Lord. This isn’t to scare the couple but to urge them to make a prayerful and informed decision about entering a lifelong relationship that will impact them over the long term. Entering marriage with eyes wide open includes spiritual preparedness and carrying realistic expectations into the relationship.

As the couple prays and discerns whether they are ready to commit to a lifelong partnership, they can better embrace the joys, responsibilities, and challenges of marriage. Candidly exploring the various facets of their relationship helps to equip the couple to face the ups and downs of married life in a God-honoring manner that combines faith and wisdom.

Engaging in Premarital Counseling

Premarital counseling prepares a couple to make informed decisions about their future. The couple will talk through their hopes and goals. Together, they will learn more about themselves, including their strengths and areas of growth as a couple. When a couple understands what marriage is like and when they prepare themselves for the reality of marriage, they can enter their future together with greater confidence.

If you’re looking to get married and build that relationship on a strong foundation, you can reach out and speak to a counselor for premarital counseling.

item.title: Sealed by God: A Therapeutic Reflection on Identity, Security, and Wholeness
item.description:
When you believed, you were marked in Him with a seal, the promised Holy Spirit… who is a guarantee of our inheritance. – Ephesians 1:13-14

Certain spiritual truths do more than inspire us – they reshape the way we see ourselves. One of those truths is the idea of being sealed by God.

I recently shared a devotional at our church where I talked about the many benefits we receive as Christians simply by asking Jesus to be Lord of our lives. One idea continued to stay with me afterward: being sealed by God.

Around that same time, I was listening to one of my favorite songs, “So Be It” by Elevation Worship. The signet ring featured on the album cover caught my attention immediately because of what I had been studying.

The first line of the song says: “When the King speaks a word, it cannot be overturned – it’s as good as done.” All of that led me to dig deeper into what it truly means to be sealed.

The Meaning of a Seal: More Than Symbolic

In ancient times, a seal carried significant authority. Kings and rulers would melt wax over a document and press their signet ring into it. That mark represented something important:

  • Ownership
  • Authority that could not be overturned
  • Authenticity
  • Protection

If a document bore the king’s seal, it was final. It was secure. It was untouchable. So, when the apostle Paul writes that believers are “sealed,” he is describing something deeply powerful. He’s describing a permanent, authoritative act of God. God has placed His mark on you, not with wax – but with His Spirit.

From a Christian counseling perspective, this matters deeply because many people walk through life feeling the exact opposite:

“I don’t belong.”
“I’m not enough.”
“Something in me is broken.”

These beliefs often stem from attachment wounds, trauma, rejection, or chronic invalidation. Over time, they can become part of a person’s core identity. But the concept of being sealed by God directly confronts those internal narratives.

Belonging: The End of Identity Confusion

To be sealed means you belong to Him – not conditionally, not temporarily, not based on performance – you are not random or overlooked; you are claimed.

Belonging is one of the most fundamental human needs. In therapy, we often explore how early experiences shape whether someone feels secure in relationships or constantly fears abandonment. When that foundation feels unstable, people may spend years trying to earn love, approval, or acceptance.

But being sealed reframes belonging as something that is given – not achieved. God says: “You are mine.” That truth has the power to quiet the internal chaos of striving. It shifts identity away from performance and toward security.

Security: Calming Anxiety at the Core

A king’s seal was not meant to be broken. It represented security and assurance. In the same way, being sealed by God speaks to security – a concept central to mental health. Anxiety often thrives in uncertainty:

“What if I fail?”
“What if I lose everything?”
“What if I don’t make it?”

These fears often reflect a nervous system that no longer feels safe.

But the seal represents a promise that cannot be undone. It reminds us that our lives are not held together by our own strength alone. A firm foundation in God can bring comfort, encouragement, and support. This does not mean we won’t have hardship or pain. But it introduces a deeper truth: you are not navigating life alone.

For those who struggle with chronic anxiety, this truth can become an anchor – something steady to return to when thoughts begin to spiral.

Approval: Healing Shame and “Damaged Goods” Thinking

One of the most powerful interpretations of the word “seal” comes from the ancient practice of placing a seal on something that had been examined and approved. That means it wasn’t defective. It wasn’t lacking. It was complete. This speaks directly to shame: the deeply rooted belief that “something is wrong with me.”

Shame often develops through experiences of criticism, rejection, trauma, or emotional neglect. Over time, these experiences can become internalized:

“I’m a mistake.”
“I’ve done too much.”
“I’ve gone too far.”
“I’m too broken.”
“I’m damaged goods.”
“If people really knew me, they wouldn’t accept me.”

But the idea of God examining and sealing you tells a different story. You are not overlooked or accidental – you are known, cared for, and intentionally marked by Him. He sees you and loves you unconditionally, not because you are perfect, but because through Christ we are fully seen, fully known, and still claimed by God.

That truth challenges the belief that you are fundamentally flawed or unworthy. From a therapeutic standpoint, this is where identity work becomes transformational. Healing often begins when people stop viewing themselves solely through the lens of their wounds and begin seeing themselves through the lens of inherent value and God-given worth.

Protection: Reframing Vulnerability

Being sealed also implies protection. Again, this does not mean life becomes easy or pain-free. Therapy reminds us that suffering is part of the human experience. Loss, disappointment, and struggle are realities of living in a fallen world.

But protection, in this sense, means that what ultimately defines you cannot be taken away. Your identity is not based on other people’s opinions; your worth is not erased by failure; your future is not determined by your past.

This can be especially meaningful for individuals who have experienced trauma or instability. When life has felt unpredictable or unsafe, the idea of divine protection can begin to rebuild a sense of internal safety.

Guarantee: Trusting the Process

In Ephesians, the seal is also described as a guarantee. One of the hardest things for many people to tolerate is uncertainty about the future. Many people find that their depression is deeply rooted in past events or that they are ruminating on their past experiences. Anxiety is often connected to fears about the future. People naturally want reassurance that everything will work out.

The idea of a guarantee offers a different kind of assurance – not that life will be perfect, but that God will not abandon what He has started. You are not abandoned. You are not left unfinished. God will faithfully carry you toward completion.

This speaks directly to the fear: “What if I don’t make it?”

The seal answers: “You will.”

Not because of flawless effort, but because of the faithful commitment of the One who placed His seal on you.

“It Is Finished”: Ending the Cycle of Striving

As we reflect on Good Friday and Easter, these ideas become even more meaningful.

When Jesus said, “It is finished,” it was not a statement of defeat. It was a declaration of completion. The work was done; the debt was paid; the mission was accomplished.

From both a psychological and spiritual perspective, many people live in a constant state of striving:

  • Trying to prove they are enough
  • Trying to fix themselves
  • Trying to earn worth or acceptance

Over time, this can lead to burnout, anxiety, and a persistent sense of inadequacy and insecurity. No matter how much you do or how much you achieve, it often still feels like it is never enough.

But “It is finished” interrupts that cycle. It reminds us that the foundation of our worth has already been established. We are not working for approval – we are living from it. Therapy can open the door to deeper healing. It can help people explore the gap between what they intellectually believe and what they emotionally carry.

Living as Someone Who Is Sealed

If you are sealed, your life can begin to reflect that reality. You do not have to prove your worth in every interaction. You do not have to crumble under criticism. You do not have to live in fear of being “found out.” You do not have to carry the weight of perfection.

Instead, you can begin moving through life with a growing sense of:

  • Stability
  • Confidence (or what I like to call “Godfidence”)
  • Peace
  • Identity
  • Security

Not because life is easy – but because you know the One who makes you secure.

Questions for Reflection

  • What voices or experiences have shaped the way you view your worth?
  • Do you tend to live from a place of striving or security?
  • What would change if you truly believed you were already loved, known, and claimed by God?
  • In moments of anxiety or shame, what would it look like to return to the truth that you are sealed by God?

Final Reflection

In his book Sparkling Gems, Rick Renner offers an interpretive translation of the Bible passage he is studying at the end of each day.

In this case, he writes that Ephesians 1:13 could be the following:

“…The moment you believed, God thoroughly examined and inspected you to make sure that you were fully intact and complete. Because He found nothing in you broken, defective, or faulty, God put His seal upon you – the ultimate proof that He found you to be impeccable. That seal meant you were approved, endorsed, recognized, affirmed, sanctified, and notarized by the Spirit of God. It was His guarantee that you are going to make it to your final destination.”

So, when doubt creeps in, when anxiety rises, when shame begins to speak, return to this truth: you are not forgotten, you are not unprotected, you are not unfinished, you are sealed. And when the King speaks, it is as good as done. “It is finished.” So be it.

item.title: Emotional Attachment: Emotional Dumping or Vulnerability?
item.description:
You’ve probably experienced it. Maybe you were on the receiving end. A friend stops by, and before you can even get past the niceties, they dump a month’s worth of their tears and fears at your feet.

Or maybe it was you. Something built up inside of you all day, all week, maybe all month, and the moment someone asked, “How are you?” it all spilled out of your mouth in one unfiltered, jarringly authentic rush.

That’s what has become popularly known as “emotional dumping.” You’ve probably heard about it on social media. There, it’s praised as equal to being vulnerable, but the truth is, emotional dumping and vulnerability are vastly different.

What really is emotional dumping?

Offloading emotions in itself isn’t a bad thing. It’s healthy for you to be transparent, to be authentic, and to show your own frailty. It’s even biblical. Being honest about your own struggles and fears makes you real, makes you humble, and emphasizes your inabilities in contrast with God’s awesome power.

But there’s a difference, a rather significant one, between sharing what’s on your heart and dumping every thought and emotion, especially to the wrong audience.

The difference isn’t necessarily in what you say

The difference between “emotional dumping” as it is popularly practiced and true vulnerability isn’t seen in the act of sharing. The difference comes more in the context and motive in which you share.

The context in which you unleash your emotions matters a lot and is directly connected to your motives. Who you’re talking to and the reasons behind it are determining factors as to whether your sharing is building a connection or creating unnecessary tension.

Is it gossip?

What often happens when you tell your story is that you’re also telling someone else’s. Because we are social creatures, we are tightly connected to one another. And while you’re entitled to tell your story, the unfortunate byproduct of this type of honesty is that you might also be telling someone else’s story, and not from a fair perspective.

Much of our stress in life comes from our interactions with other people. Maybe a friend ghosted you, and you assume that they are mad. Or your spouse said something unpleasant to you in a fit of anger, and you’re sure it’s a sign of something more sinister. While it’s tempting to “dump” your emotions onto the internet or to a willing friend, you must be careful about whom you tell and your motive for telling it.

In telling “your” story, you might also be gossiping without even realizing it. Gossip can sneak in disguised as venting, but the Bible warns us about the danger of careless words. Proverbs 18:21 sums it up nicely, “The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.” Even when your heart needs connection and communication, it’s important to be mindful of your tongue.

Is it drama?

While spilling all your emotional baggage out can be therapeutic, it can also cause and fuel drama. Life is dramatic enough without feeding into it. Maybe you’re frustrated by how clumsy you were or how forgetful. Sometimes something small happens, but by the time you retell the story, it’s had time to fester and grow.

Drama feeds on escalated emotions, and it has a way of pulling other people into your chaos unnecessarily. When you’re hurt, everything can feel magnified. And when emotions feel magnified, you can also feel compelled to overshare. Not just the factual events that happened, but also the escalation. A bad day becomes a pessimistic view of the future, or a misunderstanding escalates to certain doom.

Proverbs 29:11 tells us that “Fools give full vent to their rage, but the wise bring calm in the end” (NIV). So, wisdom is measured by how responsibly you handle what you feel. Giving in fully to your desire to vent may feel relieving in the moment, but it doesn’t always lead to resolution. Sometimes it even fuels more drama.

What’s your motive?

Are you truly looking for counsel or comfort? Are you looking to be validated? Maybe your motivation isn’t necessarily tied to wanting honest input as much as it is to seeking validation for your questionable actions. Or maybe you are looking for someone to side with you or to punish someone else who you feel has wronged you.

Is your need to share your story fueled by anger? Anger itself isn’t sinful, but the actions you take in your anger can be. Ephesians 4:26 warns against sinning in your anger. When you’re feeling angry, you might make sweeping and unfair statements. You might assign motives, thoughts, or actions to people that aren’t rooted in truth and that you can’t actually prove.

Or maybe you’re dumping your feelings out of a subtle desire to manipulate. You might not think of yourself as manipulative. Most people don’t, but if you’re telling your story in a way that pressures someone to agree with you or to turn them against someone else, your motives may not be pure.

Is it appropriate? Is it wise?

When you’re deciding to bear your soul to someone, you must first determine if it’s appropriate or wise. Just because you have an audience doesn’t mean you should tell your unfiltered story.

If you’re with someone of the opposite gender or are married (or they are), you may want to think twice before you tell your whole truth. Being transparent with someone can bond you to them and create a deep emotional attachment. And it’s important to consider who you are bonding yourself to before you do it.

You also have to take into consideration the mental and spiritual wellness of the person you’re talking with. While those who have walked through brokenness often offer good counsel, you must know if the person you’re seeking advice from supports your faith.

You also must make sure that they are strong enough to hear your story. Hearing deep emotional stories can be taxing, and if someone is struggling in their own life, that added pressure can feel like too much.

What to do instead!

If emotional dumping isn’t the right approach, what is?

This is not to discourage you from being transparent and authentic. Those qualities are often the thing that brings people together and what brings some to Christ. But it’s also important to understand the difference between emotional vomiting and healthy vulnerability.

Healthy vulnerability builds a secure emotional attachment based on mutual respect. Dumping often creates a “trauma bond” that leaves both parties exhausted.

Vulnerability simply states the events of what has happened and how they affected you. Emotional manipulation, which is often what happens when you arbitrarily “dump” your emotions on someone, is different. It not only tells the story, but it also tells the listener what they should think and feel about it.

Vulnerability desires opinions and constructive criticism. It asks for help and invites support. Dumping creates false allegiance and alliances and often comes from an impure root.

Outside Help

Healthy vulnerability also invites God into the situation. Being vulnerable also means being humble. And when you’re humble, you’re acknowledging that God is greater than your human frailty. Psalm 62:8 says, “Pour out your hearts to Him, for God is our refuge.” Notice where that pouring out is directed first. Not your friend. Not the internet. Not even your mother or your spouse.

When you release your raw, sensitive emotions to God first, something happens. Your perspective widens, and your urgency disappears. You may still want to talk to someone, and that’s entirely healthy, but you’re no longer speaking from a place of emotional combustion but from honesty and vulnerability.

Therapy, too, can be incredibly helpful because it creates a structured place that is designed for emotional exploration. The relationship with your therapist is built on emotional discovery and healing, which is a whole lot different than surprising a friend at two in the morning with an eruption of unfiltered emotion.

You don’t have to feel embarrassed afterwards or replay the conversation, wondering if you’ve overshared. You don’t have to cringe because you know you made someone uncomfortable.

If you feel like you need an “emotional dump”, please call our office to schedule an appointment with a trained professional counselor in our network. Get the help you need by calling today.
